"A comedy regarding inexplicable sexual desire, the play is an underdone mélange of farce, Greek mythological references, insult humor, and extrasensory connections.
Watching a silly comedy that most of the audience appears to be enjoying, but which you find pointless, plodding and excessively broad, can be a frustrating and bewildering experience.
But his new play drifts along, recycling themes and lines from his Oscar-winning script for 'Moonstruck,' without a destination or conclusion.
"The Portuguese Kid" is as predictable as it is old-fashioned – a hoary pseudo-romantic comedy trafficking in insulting stereotypes that died well before Don Rickles did.
But where the heart ought to be there's nothing but the shifting gears of a playwright pushing characters into outlandish situations that are rarely amusing.

Buy the ticket. The Portuguese Kid has it all: idiosyncratic characters you cannot help but champion, rambunctious dialogue that leaves you occasionally breathless, and a director's deft massage of the actors' already polished gifts for comic timing.
Shanley's feel-good romp is undoubtedly an enjoyable night out, presenting a poignant commentary on how we treat our world, how we treat each other, and ultimately, how we treat ourselves.
But it's worth a try because the audience, on the whole, responds to a lot of the silliness and laughs out loud.

“Some great acting, some rather funny dialogue, but it is short on substance...You wish for this uber talented cast and design team, a better play or at least a better sitcom. Shanley’s directing keeps his characters in a one-dimensional cardboard cartoon dimension. Luckily he cast wonderful actors who tried valiantly to climb out of that box.

Overall, though Shanley's 'The Portuguese Kid' attempts to be a hilarious battle of the sexes, its laughs are shallow and simplistic and, unfortunately, rewarding of views that don't quite sit right with our current politics.
